newsitem.title: USA: Chances improve for Senate vote on chemical pact.
newsitem.headline: Chances improve for Senate vote on chemical pact.

text.p: Prospects for an early Senate vote on an international treaty outlawing chemical weapons improved markedly on Tuesday, even as the pact was attacked by four former U.S. defence secretaries.
Senate party leaders voiced hopes that the vote would take place before April 29 when the pact comes into force.
They spoke after opponents and supporters of the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention crossed swords at a Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

"The case against this treaty can be summarized quite simply: it is not global, it is not verifiable, it is not constitutional, and it will not work," Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, said at the start of the hearing.

Former defence secretaries James Schlesinger, Caspar Weinberger and Donald Rumsfeld appeared before the committee and Dick Cheney, defence secretary under former President George Bush, argued against the treaty in a letter to Helms.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright put the administration's case, stressing the need for swift ratification.
Addressing criticism that "outlaw" states would not comply with the treaty, she said, "Those who abide by the law, not those who break it, must establish the rules by which all must be judged."
Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott told reporters Senate debate could start late next week with the idea of completing work in the April 22-24 period.
The administration has said that if the United States does not ratify before April 29, it will have no voice in the treaty's implementation.
"I don't think that date is as important a marker as the administration maintains, but I do think that we've got a chance to .. have a vote within that time frame," Lott told reporters.

Lott, who has been critical of the treaty in the past and has linked action on it to other unrelated legislation, said on Tuesday that it was "a major treaty" and efforts should be made to work out problems.
He said he could vote for or against it, depending on whether problems were worked out.

Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said that following assurances by Lott he hoped for a vote next week and was abandoning a threatened pressure tactic of holding up all Senate business until treaty action was scheduled.

The treaty bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons. Both sides in the debate have recruited long lists of critics or endorsers of the treaty from among former high officials and military officers.
Helms, flanked by two leading supporters of the treaty, Democrat Joseph Biden of Delaware and Republican Richard Lugar of Indiana, said the pact "is much worse than nothing."

He said it would increase "rogue" regimes' access to chemical agents and impose new regulations on U.S. businesses, exposing them to increased danger of industrial espionage and trampling on their constitutional rights.
"Outside the (Washington) beltway, where people don't worship at the altar of arms control, that's what we call a bum deal," Helms said.
He said negotiations with Biden on concerns about the treaty had reached agreement on about 21 "relatively minor defects" but the administration was "stonewalling" on five or six major issues.
Schlesinger said Iraq's use of poison gas had shown that treaties could do little to prevent its use or manufacture.
But Biden said the treaty would open the way to international pressure against countries with illegal chemical weapons programmes, asserting, "Norms do matter."

The Foreign Relations Committee approved the treaty on a 13-5 vote a year ago, but it was withdrawn from the full Senate in September at the administration's request after Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole opposed it, endangering prospects of getting a needed two-thirds majority.
